title: Level 2 Biology — Genetic Variation and Change (2024)
subject: biology

questions.text:
In certain breeds of domestic rabbit, ear length follows a complete dominance pattern. The allele for long ears (L) is dominant over the allele for short ears (l). A separate gene, located on a different chromosome, controls fur density. The allele for dense fur (D) is dominant to the allele for sparse fur (d).

A rabbit that is homozygous for both long ears and dense fur is crossed with a rabbit that is homozygous for both short ears and sparse fur.

State the genotype of the F1 offspring produced by this cross.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Identifies F1 genotype as LlDd.

questions.text:
Construct a Punnett square to show:
- the gametes produced by the F1 individuals and
- all possible genotypes of the F2 generation of rabbits.
questions.expectedAnswer: F1 gametes: LD, Ld, lD, ld.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Punnett square completed with correct gametes for F2.

questions.text: State the expected phenotype ratio from this F2 cross, identifying the phenotype that each value represents.
questions.expectedAnswer: 9:3:3:1 — 9 Long ears dense fur : 3 Long ears sparse fur : 3 Short ears dense fur : 1 Short ears sparse fur.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Phenotype ratio (with correct appearance/description): 9 long ears dense : 3 long ears sparse : 3 short ears dense : 1 short ears sparse.

questions.text:
In chickens, feather pattern is an example of co-dominance AND sex linkage. A gene located on the Z chromosome controls whether barred plumage (alternating light and dark bands on each feather) is present or absent. The barred allele (B) is co-dominant with the non-barred allele (b). Males can be barred, non-barred, or show partial barring if heterozygous. In birds, sex determination differs from mammals: males are ZZ and females are ZW.

Female chickens can be either barred or non-barred, but never partially barred, because they carry only one Z chromosome.

Some avian conditions are known to be sex-linked. Female birds have been found to be more susceptible to recessive, sex-linked conditions than male birds.

Evaluate the inheritance patterns in chickens, including complete dominance, co-dominance, and sex-linkage.

In your answer, refer to the examples above and include a discussion of:
- the two patterns of dominance
- why only male chickens can show partial barring
- the similarities and differences of recessive and dominant sex-linked genes.
questions.expectedAnswer: Complete dominance: one allele completely masks the other (e.g. long ears over short ears in rabbits). Co-dominance: both alleles are expressed simultaneously in the heterozygote (e.g. partial barring in ZBZb males). Sex-linkage: gene located on a sex chromosome (Z in birds). Only males (ZZ) can carry two different alleles and show the co-dominant partial barring phenotype. Females (ZW) have only one Z, so they express whichever allele is present — barred or non-barred. Recessive sex-linked conditions appear more frequently in females (ZW) because they need only one copy of the recessive allele.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Describes complete dominance.
- co-dominance.
- sex-linked gene.
- genotype of male and/or female chicken for barring.
- that males have a homologous pair of sex chromosomes (ZZ) while females have ZW.

For Merit:
- Explains why male chickens can show partial barring.
- why female chickens cannot show partial barring (only barred or non-barred).
- the difference between dominant and recessive sex-linked genes.
- why female chickens are more likely to inherit a sex-linked condition.

For Excellence:
- Discusses the co-dominant and complete dominance inheritance patterns for plumage in male and female chickens.
- dominant and recessive sex-linked genes, with reference to why females inherit recessive conditions more frequently than males.

questions.text:
The kākāpō (Strigops habroptilus) is a large, flightless parrot endemic to Aotearoa New Zealand. It is regarded as a taonga species by Ngāi Tahu and holds deep cultural significance.

Fossil evidence and genetic analysis indicate that kākāpō were once widespread across both the North and South Islands. During the Pleistocene glaciations, habitat fragmentation split kākāpō populations into isolated alpine and lowland refugia. European colonisation brought habitat destruction, introduced mammalian predators such as cats, rats, and stoats, and hunting pressure that caused a catastrophic decline in kākāpō numbers.

By the 1990s, only around 50 kākāpō remained. An intensive recovery programme was established, involving predator control, supplementary feeding, and translocation to predator-free island sanctuaries such as Whenua Hou (Codfish Island) and Anchor Island.

Genetic analyses have revealed that the surviving kākāpō population has very low genetic diversity. Some island populations established from small translocated groups show even lower variation, with certain alleles becoming fixed.

Discuss the decline in genetic diversity in the kākāpō, with reference to the information provided.

In your answer, include discussion of:
- the terms population bottleneck, founder effect, and genetic drift
- how the genetic diversity of the kākāpō gene pool has been affected by these processes
- why the reduced genetic diversity from island translocations is a concern for the kākāpō population and how conservation efforts might address this in the future.
questions.expectedAnswer: Population bottleneck: a drastic reduction in population size reducing genetic variation. Founder effect: a small group establishes a new population with only a subset of the original gene pool's alleles. Genetic drift: random changes in allele frequencies, more pronounced in small populations.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Describes population bottleneck.
- founder effect.
- genetic drift.
- gene pool.
- genetic diversity.
- a problem arising from reduced genetic diversity/reduced phenotype/inability to adapt to changing environments.
- a method of improvement for the future.

For Merit:
- Explains how genetic diversity is impacted by population bottleneck.
- how genetic diversity is impacted by founder effect.
- how genetic diversity is impacted by genetic drift.
- why the island populations are suffering the consequences of reduced/less-variable gene pools and inbreeding.
- a possible (realistic) way to improve the situation in the future.

For Excellence:
- Discusses the impacts of at least TWO of the three processes (bottleneck, founder effect, genetic drift) on genetic diversity, making reference to the information provided about the kākāpō population.
- the problems arising due to reduced genetic diversity, and a possible way that conservation could halt the decline and improve genetic diversity in the future.

questions.text:
In domestic mice, a coat-colour condition known as 'agouti' has been studied extensively. In these mice, the agouti coat-colour allele (A) is dominant to the non-agouti (black) allele (a). When agouti mice were crossed with each other (agouti x agouti), researchers observed a 2:1 phenotype ratio of agouti to black offspring, rather than the expected 3:1 ratio.

Through further test crosses, it was determined that all surviving agouti mice were heterozygous. Homozygous dominant (AA) embryos failed to develop and were reabsorbed before birth.

This is an example of lethal alleles in mammals.

Describe what is meant by the term lethal allele.
questions.expectedAnswer: A lethal allele is a version of a gene that, when present in a particular combination (e.g. homozygous dominant), prevents normal development or causes death of the organism before or shortly after birth.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Describes a lethal allele correctly.

questions.text:
Show the Punnett square for a test cross between a black mouse and a surviving agouti mouse.

Provide the genotype ratio and phenotype ratio.
questions.expectedAnswer: Cross: Aa x aa. Genotype ratio 1:1 (Aa : aa). Phenotype ratio 1:1 (agouti : black).
questions.markingGuide:
Achieved: Punnett square is correctly completed.

Both ratios are correct.

Genotype ratio 1:1 (Aa:aa).

Phenotype ratio 1:1 (agouti:black).

questions.text:
The agouti allele produces a dominant, visible phenotype in the heterozygote. However, the lethality (ability to prevent survival) is considered recessive in these mice, even though the colour phenotype is dominant.

Using the information provided, discuss why this mouse allele must be recessive for lethality and why dominant lethal alleles are rare but can still be found in some adult populations, including humans.

In your answer, include discussion of:
- the terms and meaning of dominant and recessive alleles
- why the mouse's agouti allele must be recessive for lethality and how the test cross supports this
- why dominant lethal alleles are rarer than recessive ones, but can sometimes persist in adult organisms.
questions.expectedAnswer: Dominant allele: always expressed when present, masks the recessive allele. Recessive allele: only expressed when homozygous. The lethality must be recessive because heterozygous Aa mice survive and show the agouti phenotype — only AA individuals die. If lethality were dominant, any mouse carrying even one A allele would not survive, and no agouti mice would exist.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Describes BOTH dominant and recessive alleles.
- that heterozygous individuals do not die.
- that the lethality must come later in development for dominant lethal alleles in humans.

For Merit:
- Explains how lethal alleles affect the expected ratios of individual phenotypes due to the affected individuals not surviving.
- how the test cross shows that the lethal allele must be recessive even though the colour is dominant.
- how a dominant lethal allele can exist in an adult.
- how a dominant lethal allele can be passed on, as it is expressed after reproduction has occurred.

For Excellence:
- Discusses the inheritance of coat colour for the mice, using Punnett squares/ratios to support the discussion of dominant and recessive lethal alleles.
- comparing the rarity of dominant lethal alleles to recessive alleles and their existence in adult organisms.
